blocks.body:
How do you tell whether two piles of stones have the same size without counting? Pair them off, one stone from each pile at a time, and see whether either pile runs out first. Cantor's idea was to use exactly this test for infinite sets: two sets have the same size if their elements can be paired off perfectly. The surprises start at once. The even numbers can be paired with all natural numbers ($n \leftrightarrow 2n$), so a part can be as large as the whole. Yet the real numbers cannot be paired with the natural numbers: there are genuinely different sizes of infinity.

There are two different ways to extend counting beyond the finite. Cardinals measure how many elements a set has. Ordinals measure how long a well-ordered list is, and they let induction and recursion continue past the natural numbers. This page develops both, assuming [[sets-relations]], [[functions]] (injections, surjections, bijections) and [[induction]].

blocks.title: Equinumerosity and countability
blocks.body:
Sets $A$ and $B$ are equinumerous, written $|A| = |B|$, if there is a bijection $A \to B$. We write $|A| \le |B|$ if there is an injection $A \to B$, and $|A| < |B|$ if $|A| \le |B|$ but $|A| \ne |B|$. A set is countably infinite if it is equinumerous with $\mathbb{N} = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$, countable if it is finite or countably infinite, and uncountable otherwise. The cardinality of $\mathbb{N}$ is written $\aleph_0$.

A set is countably infinite exactly when its elements can be listed as $a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots$ with every element appearing exactly once.

blocks.title: Countable sets are everywhere
blocks.body:
The integers are countable: list them as $0, -1, 1, -2, 2, \dots$, that is, send $n \in \mathbb{N}$ to $n/2$ if $n$ is even and to $-(n+1)/2$ if $n$ is odd.

The set $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ of pairs is countable. Arrange the pairs in a grid and walk along the diagonals $m + n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$ in turn. This gives the Cantor pairing function
$$\pi(m, n) = \frac{(m+n)(m+n+1)}{2} + n,$$
a bijection $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$: the pairs on earlier diagonals use up the first $\binom{m+n+1}{2}$ numbers, and $n$ gives the position on the current diagonal. By induction, $\mathbb{N}^k$ is countable for every $k$.

The rationals are countable: send each positive rational, written in lowest terms $p/q$, to the pair $(p, q)$. This is an injection into $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, so the positive rationals are infinite and inject into a countable set, hence are countable (an infinite subset of $\mathbb{N}$ can be listed in increasing order). Adding $0$ and the negatives keeps the set countable. So although the rationals are dense, there are no more of them than natural numbers.

More generally, a countable union of countable sets is countable (this needs a small amount of the axiom of choice, to pick a listing of each set). The set of all finite strings over a countable alphabet is countable, and hence so is the set of algebraic numbers (each is a root of one of countably many integer polynomials, each having finitely many roots).

blocks.title: Cantor's theorem
blocks.body: For every set $A$, there is no surjection $A \to \mathcal{P}(A)$. Hence $|A| < |\mathcal{P}(A)|$. In particular $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are uncountable.

Let $f : A \to \mathcal{P}(A)$ be any function. Consider the diagonal set
$$D = \{a \in A : a \notin f(a)\}.$$
If $D = f(d)$ for some $d \in A$, then $d \in D$ if and only if $d \notin f(d) = D$, which is impossible. So $D$ is not in the image, and $f$ is not surjective. The map $a \mapsto \{a\}$ is an injection $A \to \mathcal{P}(A)$, so $|A| \le |\mathcal{P}(A)|$, and the two are not equal.

For $\mathbb{R}$, it suffices to inject $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ into $\mathbb{R}$: send $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ to the number whose decimal expansion is $0.d_0 d_1 d_2 \dots$ with $d_n = 1$ if $n \in S$ and $d_n = 2$ otherwise. Different sets differ in some first digit, and since only the digits 1 and 2 occur, the two numbers really are different (the ambiguity $0.0999\ldots = 0.1$ needs digits 0 or 9). An uncountable set cannot inject into a countable one, so $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable.

blocks.title: Comparing sizes
blocks.body: Is $\le$ on cardinalities a sensible order? If $|A| \le |B|$ and $|B| \le |A|$, we want $|A| = |B|$. This is true but not obvious, since the two injections may have nothing to do with each other.

blocks.title: Schröder–Bernstein theorem
blocks.body: If there are injections $f : A \to B$ and $g : B \to A$, then there is a bijection $h : A \to B$.

Let $C_0 = A \setminus g(B)$, the elements of $A$ not hit by $g$, and $C_{n+1} = g(f(C_n))$. Let $C = C_0 \cup C_1 \cup C_2 \cup \cdots$. Define
$$h(x) = \begin{cases} f(x) & x \in C, \\ g^{-1}(x) & x \notin C. \end{cases}$$
This makes sense: if $x \notin C$ then $x \notin C_0$, so $x \in g(B)$, and $g^{-1}(x)$ is a single element because $g$ is injective.

Injective: $f$ is injective on $C$ and $g^{-1}$ is injective off $C$. Suppose $f(x) = g^{-1}(y)$ with $x \in C_n$ and $y \notin C$. Then $y = g(f(x)) \in C_{n+1} \subseteq C$, a contradiction.

Surjective: let $b \in B$. If $g(b) \notin C$ then $h(g(b)) = b$. If $g(b) \in C$, then $g(b) \notin C_0$ (it is in the image of $g$), so $g(b) \in C_{n+1} = g(f(C_n))$ for some $n$, and since $g$ is injective, $b = f(x)$ for some $x \in C_n$; then $h(x) = b$.

blocks.title: Cardinal arithmetic, briefly
blocks.body:
For cardinals one defines $|A| + |B| = |A \sqcup B|$ (disjoint union), $|A|\cdot|B| = |A \times B|$ and $|B|^{|A|} = |B^A|$, the set of functions $A \to B$. Since subsets of $A$ correspond to functions $A \to \{0,1\}$, $|\mathcal{P}(A)| = 2^{|A|}$. The facts above say $\aleph_0 + \aleph_0 = \aleph_0 \cdot \aleph_0 = \aleph_0$ and $|\mathbb{R}| = 2^{\aleph_0}$, the cardinality of the continuum, often written $\mathfrak{c}$. Also $\mathfrak{c} \cdot \mathfrak{c} = \mathfrak{c}$: interleaving the decimal digits of two numbers in $(0,1)$ (using expansions that do not end in repeating 9s) gives an injection $(0,1)^2 \to (0,1)$, and Schröder–Bernstein does the rest. So the plane has no more points than a line.

Is there a set of size strictly between $\aleph_0$ and $\mathfrak{c}$? The continuum hypothesis says no. Gödel (1940) and Cohen (1963) showed that it can be neither proved nor refuted from the standard Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms with choice (ZFC), if those are consistent. With the axiom of choice any two cardinalities are comparable; without it, that can fail.

blocks.title: Well-orders and ordinals
blocks.body:
Recall that a well-order is a total order in which every nonempty subset has a least element. Two well-orders have the same order type if there is an order-preserving bijection between them. Finite well-orders of the same size always have the same type, but infinite ones need not. Write $\omega$ for the type of $0 < 1 < 2 < \cdots$. Putting one extra element after all of them gives $0 < 1 < 2 < \cdots < \infty$, of type $\omega + 1$; this is not isomorphic to $\omega$, because it has a largest element. Continuing: $\omega + 2$, ..., $\omega \cdot 2$ (two copies of $\omega$ one after the other), $\omega \cdot 3$, ..., $\omega^2$ (copies of $\omega$ indexed by $\omega$), and so on. All of these are countable sets with different orders.

Von Neumann made this precise: an ordinal is a set $\alpha$ that is transitive (every element of $\alpha$ is a subset of $\alpha$) and well-ordered by $\in$. Then $0 = \varnothing$, $1 = \{0\}$, $2 = \{0, 1\}$, ..., $\omega = \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$, $\omega + 1 = \omega \cup \{\omega\}$. Each ordinal is the set of smaller ordinals. Every ordinal is either $0$, a successor $\alpha + 1 = \alpha \cup \{\alpha\}$, or a limit like $\omega$ that is neither, and every well-ordered set is isomorphic to exactly one ordinal.

Ordinal addition and multiplication are defined by concatenating orders, and they are not commutative. $1 + \omega$ (one point, then a copy of $\omega$) is again of type $\omega$, but $\omega + 1$ is not. Similarly $2 \cdot \omega$ ($\omega$ copies of a two-point order) is $\omega$, while $\omega \cdot 2 = \omega + \omega$.

blocks.title: Transfinite induction
blocks.body: Let $P(\alpha)$ be a property of ordinals. If for every ordinal $\alpha$, $P(\beta)$ for all $\beta < \alpha$ implies $P(\alpha)$, then $P(\alpha)$ holds for every ordinal $\alpha$.

If not, some ordinal fails $P$; the ordinals up to and including it are well-ordered, so there is a least ordinal $\alpha$ failing $P$. Every $\beta < \alpha$ satisfies $P$, so by hypothesis $\alpha$ does too, a contradiction. In practice one checks three cases: $0$, successors and limits, exactly as strong [[induction]] on $\mathbb{N}$, with one new kind of step.

blocks.title: Cardinals as ordinals
blocks.body: The two notions meet as follows. Using the axiom of choice, every set can be well-ordered (Zermelo's theorem), so every set is equinumerous with some ordinal. The cardinal $|A|$ is then defined as the least ordinal equinumerous with $A$. Finite cardinals are the natural numbers, and $\aleph_0 = \omega$. The ordinals $\omega, \omega+1, \omega \cdot 2, \omega^2, \dots$ are all countable and so all have cardinality $\aleph_0$; the least uncountable ordinal is $\omega_1 = \aleph_1$, then $\aleph_2$, and so on. In this language the continuum hypothesis reads $2^{\aleph_0} = \aleph_1$.

blocks.title: Explicit bijections
blocks.body:
(a) Check that $f(n) = n/2$ for even $n$ and $f(n) = -(n+1)/2$ for odd $n$ is a bijection $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$.

(b) Find the pair $(m, n)$ with $\pi(m,n) = 17$, where $\pi$ is the Cantor pairing function.
blocks.solution:
(a) Even $n$ go to $0, 1, 2, \dots$ in order, and odd $n$ go to $-1, -2, -3, \dots$ in order. Every integer is hit exactly once: $k \ge 0$ by $n = 2k$ and $k < 0$ by $n = -2k - 1$.

(b) The diagonal $s = m + n$ starts at $s(s+1)/2$: the starts are $0, 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, \dots$. Since $15 \le 17 < 21$, we have $s = 5$ and $n = 17 - 15 = 2$, $m = 3$. Check: $\pi(3, 2) = 5 \cdot 6/2 + 2 = 17$.

blocks.title: Closed and open intervals
blocks.body: Show that $[0,1]$ and $(0,1)$ have the same cardinality, first by Schröder–Bernstein and then by an explicit bijection.
blocks.solution:
Schröder–Bernstein: inclusion is an injection $(0,1) \to [0,1]$, and $x \mapsto \tfrac14 + \tfrac{x}{2}$ is an injection $[0,1] \to [\tfrac14, \tfrac34] \subseteq (0,1)$.

Explicit: use the Hilbert hotel trick on the sequence $\tfrac12, \tfrac13, \tfrac14, \dots$. Define $h : [0,1] \to (0,1)$ by
$$h(0) = \tfrac12, \quad h(1) = \tfrac13, \quad h\!\left(\tfrac1n\right) = \tfrac{1}{n+2} \ (n \ge 2), \quad h(x) = x \text{ otherwise}.$$
The points $0, 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots$ are sent onto $\tfrac12, \tfrac13, \tfrac14, \tfrac15, \dots$, each hit exactly once, and every other point is fixed. So $h$ is a bijection. Countably many points were shuffled to make room for two more.

blocks.title: An uncountable almost disjoint family
blocks.body: Call two subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ almost disjoint if their intersection is finite. Show that there are uncountably many subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ any two of which are almost disjoint.
blocks.solution:
Replace $\mathbb{N}$ by the set $T$ of finite strings of 0s and 1s, which is countably infinite (list them by length, then alphabetically), so it is enough to work in $T$. For each infinite 0-1 sequence $x = x_1 x_2 x_3 \ldots$ let $S_x \subseteq T$ be the set of its finite beginnings: the empty string, $x_1$, $x_1 x_2$, and so on.

If $x \ne y$, they first differ at some position $k$. Then $S_x$ and $S_y$ share exactly the $k$ beginnings of lengths $0, 1, \dots, k-1$, and no longer ones. So $S_x \cap S_y$ is finite. Different sequences give different sets, and by Cantor's theorem there are uncountably many infinite 0-1 sequences (they correspond to subsets of $\mathbb{N}$). This is surprising at first: one might expect an almost disjoint family to be no bigger than a disjoint one, and a family of pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ is at most countable.

blocks.body:
- "All infinite sets have the same size" is false (Cantor), and so is "a proper subset is always smaller" for infinite sets.
- Density says nothing about size: $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$ yet countable.
- In the diagonal argument with decimals, avoid the digits 0 and 9, since $0.1999\ldots = 0.2$ has two expansions.
- Ordinal and cardinal arithmetic differ: $\omega + 1 \ne \omega$ as ordinals, but $\aleph_0 + 1 = \aleph_0$ as cardinals. Ordinal addition is not commutative.
- Cantor's theorem compares $A$ with $\mathcal{P}(A)$; it does not say $\mathbb{R}$ is the next size after $\mathbb{N}$. That is the continuum hypothesis, which is independent of ZFC.

Countability is used constantly in analysis: countable sets have measure zero in [[lebesgue]] theory, and $\mathbb{R}$ being uncountable (see [[real-numbers]]) is why most real numbers are not algebraic. In [[computability]], there are countably many programs but uncountably many sets of natural numbers, so most sets are undecidable; the diagonal argument here is the same one behind the halting problem and the [[incompleteness]] theorems. The downward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem, a companion of the [[completeness-theorem]], shows every consistent countable theory has a countable model. Infinite versions of Ramsey's theorem and other results of [[infinite-combinatorics]] use cardinals and ordinals as their natural language.

1. Show that the set of all finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ is countable, while the set of all infinite subsets is uncountable.
2. Give an explicit bijection from $(0,1)$ to $\mathbb{R}$.
3. Prove that the set of real functions $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ has cardinality $2^{\mathfrak c}$, strictly larger than $\mathfrak c$.
4. Is $\omega + \omega^2$ equal to $\omega^2$? Is $\omega^2 + \omega$? Describe each order in words.
